events.title: Trump pardons Scott Jenkins, convicted sheriff, in late May 2025
events.summary: President Donald Trump pardoned Scott Jenkins, former sheriff of Culpeper County, Virginia, who had been convicted in March 2025 on federal bribery and fraud charges. Jenkins had accepted over $75,000 in bribes in exchange for "auxiliary deputy" badges that allowed unqualified recipients to carry firearms and evade regulations. Trump characterized the pardon as correcting an "overzealous Biden Department of Justice" persecution. The pardon was the first led by Ed Martin, a "Stop the Steal" advocate now heading the DOJ's Office of Pardons and "Weaponization Working Group."
events.why_relevant: The pardon of a convicted corrupt official rewards political loyalty over rule of law and undermines public trust in law enforcement and the integrity of the criminal justice system.
events.basis: During the last week of May, President Donald Trump pardoned Scott Jenkins, who had been the sheriff of Culpeper County, Virginia for 12 years, before being convicted on charges of federal bribery and fraud in March.

events.title: Supreme Court stays lower court order, allows Trump administration to revoke humanitarian parole for 532,000 migrants
events.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court issued an unsigned emergency order on Friday allowing the Trump administration to proceed with revoking temporary humanitarian parole protections granted by the Biden administration to approximately 532,000 Venezuelan, Cuban, Haitian, and Nicaraguan migrants. The decision stayed U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani's April order blocking the revocation. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor dissented, with Jackson arguing the stay would cause "needless human suffering" and expose migrants to imminent deportation or forced return to dangerous countries. events.title: SCOTUS Denied Certiorari in Nicholson v. W.L. York, Inc. (Race Discrimination in Employment)
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied certiorari in Nicholson v. W.L. York, Inc. (23-7490), a case involving alleged race discrimination by nightclub employers who barred an African American dancer from working based on racial quotas. Justice Jackson, joined by Justice Sotomayor, dissented from the denial, arguing that the Fifth Circuit's ruling was "patently erroneous" under established precedent (National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan) that each discrete discriminatory act restarts the statute of limitations clock. Jackson contended that Nicholson's claims of being denied access in November 2017 and August 2021 were timely and independently actionable, regardless of earlier discrimination.
events.why_relevant: The denial leaves in place a Fifth Circuit ruling that narrows remedies for victims of repeated race discrimination by treating recent discriminatory acts as mere "continued effects" of older conduct, potentially weakening Title 42 U.S.C. §1981 protections and limiting access to courts for workers facing ongoing racial exclusion.
events.basis: The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied. JUSTICE JACKSON, with whom JUSTICE SOTOMAYOR joins, dissenting from the denial of certiorari.

events.title: SCOTUS Denied Certiorari in Snope v. Brown (Maryland AR-15 Ban)
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied certiorari in Snope v. Brown (24-203), a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland's ban on AR-15 semi-automatic rifles. Justices Alito and Gorsuch would have granted the petition. Justice Kavanaugh issued a statement noting that millions of Americans own AR-15s, 41 of 50 states permit them, and petitioners have "a strong argument" that AR-15s are in "common use" and thus protected under Heller. Kavanaugh stated the Fourth Circuit's decision upholding the ban is "questionable" under existing precedent and predicted the Court will address the AR-15 issue "soon, in the next Term or two."
events.why_relevant: The denial leaves Maryland's AR-15 ban intact for now, but Kavanaugh's statement signals likely future Supreme Court review and potential invalidation of state-level semi-automatic rifle restrictions, with implications for state gun-control authority and Second Amendment scope.
events.basis: The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied. JUSTICE ALITO and JUSTICE GORSUCH would grant the petition for a writ of certiorari. Statement of JUSTICE KAVANAUGH respecting the denial of certiorari.

events.title: FDA classifies bacterial protease detection device for chronic wounds as Class II
events.summary: The Food and Drug Administration issued a final order classifying the WOUNDCHEK Bacterial Status device—a lateral flow in vitro diagnostic device designed to detect bacterial protease activity in chronic wound fluid—into Class II (special controls). The classification became effective June 2, 2025, though it was applicable retroactively to December 2, 2019.

events.title: National Weather Service loses 600 employees and faces operational gaps
events.summary: Cuts to the National Weather Service, part of NOAA, have resulted in the loss of more than 600 employees. Fifteen NWS offices on the Gulf of Mexico, a region vulnerable to hurricanes, are now understaffed. Miami's National Hurricane Center is short five specialists. Thirty of the 122 NWS stations no longer have a meteorologist in charge, and as of June 1, seven of those 122 stations lack sufficient staff to operate around the clock. Earlier cuts had already reduced weather balloon deployments, creating data gaps that affected forecasting for a March ice storm in Northern Michigan and April storms and floods in Oklahoma.
events.why_relevant: The loss of critical weather forecasting capacity during hurricane season directly threatens public safety and the ability of the National Weather Service to provide the estimated $31.5 billion in annual economic benefits from weather forecasts.
events.basis: 15 NWS offices on the Gulf of Mexico, a region vulnerable to hurricanes, are understaffed after losing more than 600 employees. Miami's National Hurricane Center is short five specialists.

The CBO score aligns with estimates from a wide range of economists and think tanks, though Republicans have attacked the CBO's credibility in response.
events.why_relevant: Congressional Budget Office fiscal scoring of major legislation provides independent analysis of budgetary impact and informs legislative debate on fiscal responsibility.
events.basis: the CBO's analysis of the Republicans' 'One Big, Beautiful Bill' is that it will add $2.4 trillion to the deficit over the next decade because the $1.2 trillion in spending cuts in the measure do not fully offset the $3.7 trillion in tax cuts for the wealthy and corporations.

events.title: Elon Musk publicly opposed Trump's omnibus spending bill
events.summary: Billionaire Elon Musk, who holds a position in the federal government, posted on X in opposition to Trump's "One Big, Beautiful Bill," calling it "a disgusting abomination" and "massive, outrageous, pork-filled." Musk's statement contradicted Trump's earlier attack on Senator Rand Paul for opposing the bill's cost. The post signaled internal disagreement within the Trump administration over fiscal policy and Musk's willingness to publicly challenge Trump on major legislative priorities.
events.why_relevant: The public disagreement between Trump and Musk over spending priorities demonstrates fractures within the administration and Musk's independent influence over policy despite his subordinate position.

President Trump refused to back the legislation, effectively stalling it in the Senate. This refusal occurred despite Trump's public statements expressing frustration with Putin and despite the ongoing Russian military escalation against Ukraine.
events.why_relevant: Trump's refusal to support bipartisan sanctions legislation undermines congressional efforts to pressure Russia and signals continued executive preference for negotiation over enforcement of consequences for Russian aggression.

events.title: White House releases promotional framing of "One Big Beautiful Bill" legislation
events.summary: The White House issued a release compiling X posts by Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller promoting the "One Big Beautiful Bill" (BBB), which the administration characterizes as essential legislation combining border security, deportation measures, tax cuts, and spending reforms. Miller argues the bill represents a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to deliver on Trump's core promises and claims it will increase "by orders of magnitude" the removal of undocumented and criminal aliens. The release frames the bill as achievable only through reconciliation (50-vote threshold) and positions it as the administration's vehicle for simultaneous tax, immigration, and welfare policy changes.

events.basis: The BBB will increase by orders of magnitude the scope, scale and speed of removing illegal and criminal aliens from the United States. For that reason alone, it's the most essential piece of legislation currently under consideration in the entire Western World, in generations.

events.title: US Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rules San Diego yoga ordinance unconstitutional
events.summary: A three-judge panel of the US Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on Wednesday overturned a San Diego municipal ordinance that banned yoga classes of four or more people at shoreline parks and beaches. The court ruled that the ordinance violated the First Amendment rights of instructors Steven Hubbard and Amy Baack, finding that teaching yoga constitutes protected speech. San Diego had argued the restriction targeted commercial activity rather than speech, citing park preservation and safety concerns. By Thursday, Hubbard resumed teaching yoga classes at Pacific Beach park.
events.why_relevant: The ruling protects First Amendment expressive activity and rejects a municipal attempt to restrict public assembly and speech, affirming judicial oversight of local ordinances that burden constitutional rights.

events.title: Federal judge temporarily halts deportation of Colorado fire attack suspect's family
events.summary: US District Judge Gordon Gallagher in Colorado issued a temporary restraining order on Wednesday blocking the Trump administration from deporting the family of Mohamed Sabry Soliman, charged in a Boulder firebombing attack. Soliman's wife and five children were taken into federal custody by immigration authorities on Tuesday after Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced their detention. Family lawyers argued the detention violated due process and constituted unlawful collective punishment of relatives for a suspect's alleged crime.

events.title: Two Chinese scientists charged with smuggling Fusarium graminearum fungus into US
events.summary: Yunqing Jian, 33, and Zunyong Liu, 34, were charged by the US Department of Justice with conspiracy, smuggling, false statements, and visa fraud for allegedly smuggling Fusarium graminearum, a toxic fungus classified as a "potential agroterrorism weapon," into the United States. Liu was intercepted at Detroit airport in July 2024 with plant material in his backpack; Jian was arrested and held pending a bond hearing. The fungus causes crop losses worth billions annually and serious illness in humans and livestock. The pair allegedly planned to conduct research at a University of Michigan laboratory where Jian worked.
events.why_relevant: The case reflects escalating US-China tensions and demonstrates law enforcement action against alleged bioterrorism threats, with national security implications for agricultural infrastructure and public health.

events.summary: The US Supreme Court unanimously vacated a lower court decision and remanded the case of Marlean Ames, an Ohio state employee who claimed she was denied promotion because she is heterosexual. The ruling eliminates a heightened evidentiary standard that had required majority-group plaintiffs to demonstrate employer discrimination against their group before pursuing Title VII civil rights claims. events.title: FCC adopts revised methodology for assessing space and earth station regulatory fees effective fiscal year 2025
events.summary: The Federal Communications Commission adopted targeted amendments to its regulatory fee methodology for space and earth station operators. Key changes include assessing fees when stations are authorized rather than when operational, and splitting Non-Geostationary Orbit (NGSO) space station categories into small constellations (fewer than 1,000 authorized stations) and large constellations (1,000 or more), replacing the prior "less complex" and "other" categories. The 60/40 allocation between small and large constellations aims to lower per-unit fees for most operators while broadening the fee-payor base.

The order mandates the FAA issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking within 18 months to define acceptable noise thresholds for supersonic aircraft operations and complete final rulemaking within 24 months. It also directs the Office of Science and Technology Policy to coordinate federal research and development efforts and instructs the Secretary of Transportation to engage international aviation authorities on harmonized supersonic regulatory approaches.
events.why_relevant: The order removes a longstanding regulatory barrier through executive action, reassigning authority over noise and safety standards from established law to agency rulemaking, and represents an assertion of executive power to override decades of environmental and noise-protection policy through expedited regulatory reform.
events.basis: The Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) shall take the necessary steps, including through rulemaking, to repeal the prohibition on overland supersonic flight in 14 CFR 91.817 within 180 days of the date of this order.
events.action: announced an executive order titled "Leading The World in Supersonic Flight"

events.title: SCOTUS denies certiorari in Chambers-Smith v. Ayers; Alito and Thomas issue statement criticizing Sixth Circuit habeas ruling
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied certiorari in Chambers-Smith v. Ayers (No. 24–584), a case involving Kayla Ayers's federal habeas petition claiming ineffective assistance of counsel in her 2013 arson and child endangerment conviction. Justice Alito, joined by Justice Thomas, issued a statement criticizing the Sixth Circuit's reversal of the District Court's denial of the habeas petition as untimely. Alito argued the Sixth Circuit erred by treating a newly discovered 2019 expert fire-inspection report as sufficient to restart the one-year limitations period under 28 U.S.C. §2244(d)(1)(D), when the factual predicate for the ineffective-assistance claim existed at trial in 2013. Alito noted that Ayers has since completed her sentence and is no longer subject to post-release control, making the case moot as to her, but cautioned lower courts not to construe the denial as approval of the Sixth Circuit's decision.
events.why_relevant: The statement signals judicial disagreement over habeas corpus access and the interpretation of statutory limitations periods in post-conviction relief, with implications for prisoners' ability to challenge convictions based on newly discovered evidence of counsel ineffectiveness.
events.basis: The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied. Statement of JUSTICE ALITO, with whom JUSTICE THOMAS joins, respecting the denial of certiorari.
